title: The sensory unit and its receptive field
objective: Define a sensory unit and relate receptive-field size to acuity.

steps.title: One neuron, one territory
steps.body: A **[[sensory unit]]** is one sensory neuron plus all the endings it branches into. The patch of body it covers is its **[[receptive field]]**. Small receptive fields packed densely give fine spatial detail; large ones give coarse, blurry localization.

steps.prompt: A region has many neurons, each with a tiny receptive field. What does that give?
options: High spatial acuity, with fine localization
Poor localization but noticeably faster speed
Faster conduction, but no change in acuity
Coarser localization, since the fields overlap
steps.explanation: Many small, dense receptive fields let the brain pinpoint *where* a stimulus is — like a high-resolution grid.

variants.setup: Skin region A has tiny, dense receptive fields; region B has large ones.
variants.reveal: Small, dense receptive fields give finer spatial resolution, so region A localizes better.

steps.setup: A single afferent branches to cover a very large area of tissue.
steps.prompt: What do you predict about localizing a stimulus in that area?
options: Poor localization — the brain only knows 'somewhere in that field'
Very precise localization, right down to the exact spot that was touched
Normal localization, as long as the axon is myelinated
steps.reveal: One neuron covering a big field can't tell the brain *where* within it a stimulus fell — only that it fired. Large fields = coarse localization. This idea explains visceral sensation (next unit).

variants.prompt: A big receptive field means localization is…
variants.explanation: A large field can't resolve position within it, so localization is coarse.

steps.title: Convergence blurs further
steps.body: If many afferents **[[converge]]** onto one central neuron, the brain sees their fields merged into one bigger effective field — more sensitivity, less precision. The nervous system constantly trades acuity against coverage.

sources.note: The sensory neurons of touch: fiber classes, receptive fields, the sensory unit.
